cues.text: Let us now turn to the case study for this session, the University of National Tech, which we will refer to as UNTech.
UNTech is a university facing four connected problems.
First, its online learning is growing, so more and more teaching depends on the network.
Second, it suffers exam congestion, meaning the network becomes overloaded at the times when students are sitting examinations.
Third, it has inefficient allocation, which means network resources are not being shared out well between the people and services that need them.
And fourth, it faces security challenges.
Now, the case is presented as an educational case, and it brings together several of the technologies we have studied.
Let me take them in the order the case gives them.
It uses VLAN-based virtual networks.
A VLAN lets one physical network be divided into separate logical networks, so different groups of users can be kept apart.
It uses centrally managed SDN traffic policies.
In software-defined networking, the rules for handling traffic are managed from a central point, rather than being configured device by device.
It uses cloud networking and SD-WAN, which connect the university to cloud services and to its other sites.
It uses redundancy and load balancing.
Redundancy means having backup components or paths, and load balancing means spreading traffic across them.
It uses VPNs, or virtual private networks, for protected connections.
It uses IDS and IPS, that is, intrusion detection systems and intrusion prevention systems, which watch for hostile activity.
And it uses Zero Trust, the security approach in which no user or device is trusted automatically.

The goal of putting all of this together is twofold: dynamic allocation, so that resources can be assigned as demand changes, and safer isolation, so that different parts of the network are better separated from one another.
The case then tells us what to assess, and I want you to treat this as a checklist.
You should assess controller resilience, which asks what happens if the central SDN controller fails or becomes unavailable.
You should assess remote-access dependencies, which asks how much the university relies on remote connections such as VPNs.
You should assess failure modes, meaning the different ways the design could break.
You should assess policy correctness, which asks whether the traffic and security policies actually do what they are meant to do.
And you should assess costs.
There is one more point, and it is an important one.
Peak examination traffic requires capacity planning, not simply prioritisation.
In other words, giving exam traffic higher priority is not enough on its own.
If the network does not have enough capacity for the peak load, prioritising some traffic does not create the missing capacity.
The capacity itself has to be planned for.
Finally, a necessary qualification: the case outcomes are illustrative claims.
They are presented as examples to learn from, not as proven results.
